eco-01.title: Scarcity and Choice
explain: Economics starts from **scarcity**. Scarcity is the condition in which the resources available (time, money, labor, land, and so on) are insufficient relative to what people want. Whether or not one is rich, a day has only 24 hours, so scarcity applies to everyone. Because resources are limited, we must make **choices**, and choosing one thing means giving up another.

Among the things given up when making a choice, the one with the greatest value is called the **opportunity cost**. It does not add up all the alternatives forgone; only **the single best one** counts. If you watch a movie on a Saturday afternoon, the opportunity cost is the best other thing you could have done with that time.

A society's choices can be drawn as a **production possibility frontier**. It is a line connecting the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with given resources and technology. Below is a fictional island that produces only fish and coconuts.

explain.alt: A production possibility frontier for a fictional island producing fish (horizontal axis, 0 to 4 fish) and coconuts (vertical axis, 0 to 10 coconuts). The points on the curve are A (fish 0, coconuts 10), B (1, 9), C (2, 7), D (3, 4), and E (4, 0), and the curve bends downward to the right. A square point F (fish 1, coconuts 3) lies inside the curve, and a triangle point G (fish 3, coconuts 8) lies outside the curve.
explain.caption: Production possibility frontier of a fictional island

explain:
- Points on the curve (A to E) are combinations that use resources fully. To get more of one good, you must give up some of the other.
- A point inside the curve (F) is a combination that can be produced but leaves resources idle or wasted.
- A point outside the curve (G) cannot be produced with the current resources and technology.

The curve bends more and more steeply downward to the right because the more fish are produced, the more coconuts must be given up. Resources best suited to fish are used first, and later, resources better suited to coconuts have to be shifted over.

examples.title: Moving along the curve
body: Going from A to B, we gain 1 more fish but give up 10 − 9 = 1 coconut. The opportunity cost of 1 fish is 1 coconut.
Going from D to E, we gain 1 more fish but give up 4 − 0 = 4 coconuts. For the same 1 fish, the opportunity cost has become four times as large.

eco-02.title: Demand and Supply
explain: In a market, the price is determined by the forces of those who want to buy and those who want to sell. Let us look at the coffee market of a fictional town. When the price rises, the quantity buyers want falls, and when the price rises, the quantity sellers want to sell increases.

- **Quantity demanded**: the amount consumers want to buy at a given price. Other things being equal, it falls as the price rises (the law of demand).
- **Quantity supplied**: the amount producers want to sell at a given price. Other things being equal, it rises as the price rises.
Writing the town's quantity demanded and quantity supplied (in cups) as functions of the price $P$ (in thousands of won) gives the following.

explain.alt: A graph of price (vertical axis, thousand won) and quantity (horizontal axis, cups). The green demand curve slopes down from a price of 5 thousand won at 10 cups to a price of 1 thousand won at 90 cups, and the orange supply curve slopes up from a price of 1 thousand won at 10 cups to a price of 5 thousand won at 90 cups. Dotted lines from the point where the two lines meet indicate a price of 3 thousand won and a quantity of 50 cups.
explain.caption: Coffee market of a fictional town

explain: At the point where the two curves meet, the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers want. The price at that point is the **equilibrium price**, and the quantity is the **equilibrium quantity**. In equations, $Q_d = Q_s$, so $110 - 20P = 20P - 10$, that is, $P = 3$, and the quantity traded is 50 cups.

When the price is above equilibrium, the quantity sellers want exceeds the quantity buyers want, creating a **surplus** (excess supply) and downward pressure on the price. When the price is below equilibrium, there is a **shortage** (excess demand) and upward pressure on the price. Through such pressures the market moves toward equilibrium.

When factors other than price (such as consumers' income or tastes, or the cost of materials) change, the whole curve shifts. For example, if a coffee craze raises demand, the demand curve shifts to the right, and both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity increase.

The quantity sellers want is 40 cups greater, so there is a surplus, and the price will fall.

eco-03.title: Elasticity
explain: We have learned that the quantity demanded falls when the price rises. But by how much? **Price elasticity** measures the size of this response. The price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price (we drop the sign and look only at the magnitude). In the formula below, the numerator 수요량 변화율 means the percentage change in quantity demanded, and the denominator 가격 변화율 means the percentage change in price. In the formula below, the numerator 수요량 변화율 means the percentage change in quantity demanded, and the denominator 가격 변화율 means the percentage change in price.
$$E_d = \frac{\text{수요량 변화율(\%)}}{\text{가격 변화율(\%)}}$$
A percentage change is the change as a proportion of the starting value. If the price goes from 1,000 won to 1,100 won, it has risen by $\frac{100}{1000} = 10\%$.

- $E_d > 1$: **elastic**. The quantity changes by more than the price does.
- $E_d < 1$: **inelastic**. The quantity changes by less than the price does.
- $E_d = 1$: the percentage changes are equal.

explain.alt: Two demand curve diagrams. The left 'elastic' diagram has a gently sloping line, and when the price rises by the same amount from p1 to p2, the interval of quantity change is long (a large quantity change). The right 'inelastic' diagram has a steeply sloping line, and for the same price change the interval of quantity change is short (a small quantity change).
explain.caption: The same price change, different quantity responses

explain: Goods with many substitutes or that are not essential tend to be elastic, while goods with few substitutes that are essential to daily life tend to be inelastic. These are only tendencies, and even the same good becomes more elastic as time passes and alternatives appear.

Elasticity is also linked to a seller's revenue (price × quantity sold). When demand is elastic, raising the price cuts the quantity by more, so revenue falls; when demand is inelastic, raising the price raises revenue. This is a fictional calculation and not advice on actual pricing.

eco-04.title: Costs
explain: To decide how much to make, a firm needs to know its costs. Let us look at the cost (in units of 10,000 won) of a fictional bakery according to the number of trays of bread it bakes per day (output $q$).

- **Fixed cost**: cost incurred regardless of output (such as the shop's monthly rent). For this bakery it is 20.
- **Variable cost**: cost that changes with output (flour, packaging, and so on).
- **Total cost** $TC$ = fixed cost + variable cost.
The bakery's total costs for $q = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ are 20, 30, 38, 45, 54, 65, 80 respectively. From these we calculate two more costs.

- **Average cost**: cost per tray. $AC = \dfrac{TC}{q}$
- **Marginal cost**: the increase in total cost from making one more tray. $MC = TC(q) - TC(q-1)$

explain.alt: A graph of the fictional bakery's output (horizontal axis, 1 to 6 trays) and cost (vertical axis, in 10,000 won). The average cost, shown by green circles, falls through 30, 19, 15, 13.5, 13, and about 13.3, rising slightly at the end. The marginal cost, shown by orange squares, is 10, 8, 7, 9, 11, and 15, first falling and then rising quickly.
explain.caption: Average cost and marginal cost of a fictional bakery

explain: At first, average cost falls quickly because the fixed cost is spread over more trays, and it rises again once marginal cost becomes greater than average cost. When marginal cost is **lower** than average cost, average cost falls, and when it is **higher**, average cost rises. This is because an average is pulled toward the value newly added.
Marginal cost is the cost of 'one more,' so it plays an important role in a firm's production decisions, but the detailed theory lies outside the scope of this lesson.

Marginal cost: $TC(3) - TC(2) = 45 - 38 = 7$. Marginal cost is lower than average cost, so this is a range in which average cost is falling.

eco-05.title: Market Failure
explain: Markets often allocate resources well through price signals. But sometimes leaving things to the market does not produce good results for society as a whole, and this is called **market failure**. Let us look at two representative causes.

**1. Externalities.** An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on a third party who is not a party to the transaction. When it imposes a cost, it is a **negative externality**. If a fictional dye factory on a riverbank pollutes the river, it is the residents, not those who buy and sell the cloth, who suffer the harm. In this case the **social cost** borne by society is greater than the **private cost** paid by the factory.

explain.alt: A graph of price (vertical axis, 2 to 12) and quantity (horizontal axis, 0 to 9). The green demand curve slopes down from a price of 12 at quantity 0 to a price of 3 at quantity 9. The orange private cost curve starts at a price of 2 at quantity 0 and rises to the upper right, and the dotted social cost curve starts at a price of 4 at quantity 0 and rises above it with the same slope. The orange point is at quantity 5 (market) and the black point is at quantity 4 (optimum).
explain.caption: A fictional market with an externality

explain: In the figure, the market trades at quantity 5, where demand meets private cost. But if we take the social cost, which includes the external harm, as the standard, quantity 4 is appropriate. With a negative externality, the market produces **more** than the amount that suits society. Conversely, with a positive externality (for example, the benefit of vaccination spreading to those around), the market produces too little.

**2. Public goods.** These are goods with two properties. **Non-excludability** means it is hard to keep out people who have not paid, and **non-rivalry** means that one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others. Under these conditions, **free riding** arises, in which everyone expects others to pay and does not pay themselves, so the market tends not to supply enough. A lighthouse in a fictional village is an example.

There are several ways to reduce these problems, and each has advantages and disadvantages. Taxes or charges preserve the price signal but make it hard to set the right amount. Direct regulation is certain but has difficulty reflecting the different circumstances of each firm. Negotiation between the parties is possible only when its costs are low. Government intervention may also fall short of expectations because of lack of information or enforcement costs, so debate continues over which method is better, depending on circumstances and value judgments.

eco-06.title: Introduction to Macroeconomics
explain: So far we have looked at a single market. **Macroeconomics** looks at a country's production, prices, and jobs all at once. We introduce two tools.

**GDP (gross domestic product)** is the sum of the **market value of final goods and services** newly produced within a country over a given period. If intermediate goods were added separately, the same value would be counted several times, so we either count only final goods or add up the **value added** at each stage (sales − cost of purchased materials). The two give the same value.

explain.alt: Three boxes of a fictional village connected by arrows. The farmer (wheat) has sales of 30 and value added of 30, the mill (flour) has sales of 50 and value added of 20, and the bakery (bread) has sales of 80 and value added of 30. Below it is written 'Final good bread 80 = sum of value added 30 + 20 + 30', and the unit is 10,000 won.
explain.caption: From wheat to bread in a fictional village

explain: In the figure, the bread worth 80 is the final good. Adding the farmer's 30, the mill's 50 − 30 = 20, and the bakery's 80 − 50 = 30 gives 80. Adding up all the sales gives 30 + 50 + 80 = 160, in which the wheat and the flour are each counted twice.

A **price index** shows how the price of a fixed basket of goods has changed relative to a base period. The base year is set to 100. If a basket that cost 50,000 won in the base year costs 53,000 won this year, the index is $\dfrac{53000}{50000} \times 100 = 106$.

**Inflation** is a sustained rise in the price level, measured by the rate of change of the price index (in the formula below, 인플레이션율 is the inflation rate, 올해 지수 is this year's index, and 작년 지수 is last year's index).
$$\text{인플레이션율} = \frac{\text{올해 지수} - \text{작년 지수}}{\text{작년 지수}} \times 100\%$$
When prices rise, the same money buys less. So even if wages rise, purchasing power falls if prices rise by more. All figures in this lesson are fictional.

If last year's index is 106 and this year's is 111.3, it is $\frac{5.3}{106} \times 100\% = 5\%$.

eco-07.title: Consumer Choice Theory: Indifference Curves and Substitution and Income Effects
explain: To explain why the demand curve slopes downward, we must start from how a consumer maximizes satisfaction (utility) with a limited income. The **budget line** $P_X X + P_Y Y = M$ is the set of maximum bundles that can be bought given income $M$ and the prices of the two goods $P_X, P_Y$, and the absolute value of its slope is the relative price $P_X / P_Y$.

An **indifference curve** is a line connecting the combinations $(X, Y)$ that give the consumer the same utility. To obtain one more unit of $X$, the amount of $Y$ the consumer is willing to give up is called the **marginal rate of substitution** (MRS $= MU_X / MU_Y$). Because of diminishing marginal utility, indifference curves are convex to the origin, and the MRS gets smaller as one moves down along the curve.

The **utility-maximization condition** at an interior solution is the point where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line, that is, $MRS = \frac{MU_X}{MU_Y} = \frac{P_X}{P_Y}$ or $\frac{MU_X}{P_X} = \frac{MU_Y}{P_Y}$. Total utility is maximized when the additional satisfaction gained is the same whichever good the last won is spent on.

explain.alt: A diagram of the tangency of indifference curves and budget lines. When the price of good X falls, the move from the initial equilibrium A (X=4) to the compensated equilibrium B (X=7) is the substitution effect (+3), and the move to the final equilibrium C (X=11) is the income effect (+4), so the total price effect is +7.
explain.caption: The total effect of a price fall is the sum of the substitution effect from the change in relative prices and the income effect from the increase in real purchasing power.

explain: When the price of good $X$ falls, the change in consumption (the price effect) splits into two channels. First, the **substitution effect** (A→B), in which the consumer buys more of the relatively cheaper $X$ while keeping the original utility level, always works in the direction opposite to the price. Second, the **income effect** (B→C), which reflects the increase in real income caused by the lower price, raises consumption for a normal good and lowers it for an inferior good.

If, for an inferior good, the income effect is so large that it overwhelms even the substitution effect, a **Giffen good** appears, for which the quantity consumed actually falls when the price falls. However, Giffen goods are close to a theoretical exception, and for most goods the substitution effect dominates, so the law of demand holds.

examples.title: Finding the utility-maximizing bundle
body: The utility function is $U(X, Y) = X Y$, so $MRS = Y / X$, and the prices are $P_X = 10$, $P_Y = 5$ and income is $M = 100$.
Step 1: The tangency condition $Y / X = 10 / 5 = 2$ gives $Y = 2X$. Step 2: Substituting into the budget line $10X + 5(2X) = 100$ gives $20X = 100$, so $X^* = 5, Y^* = 10$.
Interpretation: When 50 won is spent on each of the two goods, the ratios of marginal utility to price are equal and satisfaction is maximized.

Step 1: The substitution effect is $7 - 4 = +3$. Step 2: The income effect is $11 - 7 = +4$.
Interpretation: Consumption rose by 4 when real income rose, so this good is a normal good, and the total price effect is +7.

eco-08.title: Producer Theory and Short-Run and Long-Run Equilibrium in Perfect Competition
explain: A firm uses labor ($L$) and capital ($K$) as inputs to produce output ($Q$). In the short run, capital is fixed, so as labor keeps being increased the **law of diminishing marginal product** operates, with the additional output becoming smaller and smaller. This is why **marginal cost** (MC $= \Delta TC / \Delta Q$), the cost of increasing output by one more unit, slopes upward beyond a certain level.

Total cost (TC) is the sum of fixed cost (FC) and variable cost (VC), and dividing by output gives average total cost ($ATC = AFC + AVC$). **The marginal cost (MC) curve always passes through the minimum points of average variable cost (AVC) and average total cost (ATC) from below.** This is because a marginal value pulls the average down when it is smaller than the average and pulls it up when it is larger.

An individual firm in a **perfectly competitive market** is a price taker, accepting the market price $P$ as given, so marginal revenue equals price ($MR = P$). Therefore the profit-maximizing output is determined where **$P = MC$**.

In the short run, even if there is a loss, fixed cost is already a sunk cost, so if the price $P$ is higher than the minimum of average variable cost ($P \ge \min AVC$), it is advantageous to keep operating and recover at least part of the fixed cost. Conversely, **if $P < \min AVC$, shutting down immediately (the shutdown point)** minimizes the loss.

In the long run, all costs are variable and firms can freely enter and exit. If there is a positive economic profit, new firms enter, market supply increases, and the price falls, so the long-run equilibrium converges to a state of zero economic profit (only normal profit) at **$P = MC = \min LAC$**.

examples.title: Short-run profit maximization and calculating total profit
body: A perfectly competitive firm's total cost is $TC(Q) = Q^2 + 4Q + 16$, so marginal cost is $MC = 2Q + 4$. The market price is $P = 20$.
Step 1: From $P = MC$, $20 = 2Q + 4$, so the optimal output is $Q^* = 8$. Step 2: Total revenue is $TR = 20 \times 8 = 160$ and total cost is $TC = 64 + 32 + 16 = 112$.
Interpretation: The maximized short-run profit is 160 - 112 = 48.

Step 1: If it operates, total revenue is 180 and total cost is 250, so the loss is 70. Step 2: If it stops operating, it loses the entire fixed cost of 100.
Interpretation: Since P (18) > AVC (15), it is rational in the short run to keep operating while bearing the loss (70).

eco-09.title: Monopoly Deadweight Loss and Game Theory in Oligopoly
explain: A **monopolist**, the only supplier in a market, faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve. To sell one more unit, it must lower the price on all earlier units as well, so **marginal revenue (MR) is always lower than price (P)**. For the linear inverse demand curve $P = a - bQ$, differentiating total revenue $TR = aQ - bQ^2$ gives $MR = a - 2bQ$, whose slope is exactly twice that of the demand curve.

The monopolist sets output where **$MR = MC$**, namely $Q_m$, and then charges the maximum price $P_m$ that consumers are willing to pay at that quantity, read off the demand curve. As a result, compared with perfect competition ($P = MC$), **output is lower and the price is higher**, part of consumer surplus is transferred to monopoly profit, and the reduction in the quantity traded creates a **deadweight loss** that goes to no one.

explain.alt: A diagram of monopoly market equilibrium. With demand P=100-2Q, marginal revenue MR=100-4Q, and marginal cost MC=20, the monopoly equilibrium is Qm=20, Pm=60, which yields a monopoly profit of 800, and compared with perfect competition (Qc=40, Pc=20) there is a deadweight loss (DWL) equal to a triangle of area 400.
explain.caption: A monopolist restricts output where MR=MC and raises the price, which causes inefficiency in resource allocation (deadweight loss).

explain: In an **oligopoly**, where a small number of firms compete, strategic interaction that takes the rivals' responses into account is the key, so it is analyzed with **game theory**. The point where each firm's strategy maximizes its own payoff given the other's fixed strategy is called a **Nash equilibrium**.

A strategy that is always better for oneself whatever the other chooses is called a **dominant strategy**. If two oligopolists collude and cut production, they can share monopoly profit, but if each follows the dominant strategy of secretly expanding output, the collusion eventually breaks down and both firms are left with low profits, falling into the **prisoner's dilemma**.

examples.title: Calculating monopoly price, output, and deadweight loss
body: Market inverse demand is $P = 100 - 2Q$, and the monopolist's marginal cost is $MC = 20$ (fixed cost 0).
Step 1: From $MR = 100 - 4Q = 20$, $Q_m = 20$, and substituting into the demand equation gives $P_m = 60$. Step 2: The perfectly competitive output comes from $100 - 2Q_c = 20$, giving $Q_c = 40$.
Interpretation: The deadweight loss is $\frac{1}{2} \times (60 - 20) \times (40 - 20) = 400$.

examples.title: An oligopoly price-cutting game and Nash equilibrium

Step 1: When the rival chooses a high price, a low price is better for me (70 > 50). Step 2: When the rival chooses a low price, a low price is again better for me (25 > 10), so 'low price' is the dominant strategy.
Interpretation: The only Nash equilibrium is (low, low), and each earns 2.5 billion won, which is worse than the joint best (5 billion won).

eco-10.title: Short-Run Macro Model I: IS-LM, the Multiplier, and Crowding Out
explain: In the short-run macroeconomy, the framework that shows how national income ($Y$) and the interest rate ($r$) are determined simultaneously when the price level is fixed is the **IS-LM model**. The **IS curve** represents equilibrium in the goods market ($Y = C(Y - T) + I(r) + G$), and it **slopes downward** because investment increases and national income rises only when the interest rate falls.

When the interest rate is fixed, if government spending rises by $\Delta G$, then through a chain of expanded consumption driven by the marginal propensity to consume ($c$), income increases by $\frac{1}{1 - c}\Delta G$. This is called the **simple multiplier effect of fiscal policy**, and the IS curve shifts to the right by that amount.

The **LM curve** represents equilibrium in the money market ($M / P = L(Y, r)$). When national income $Y$ rises, the transactions demand for money increases, and if the real money supply ($M/P$) is fixed, the interest rate $r$ must rise to keep the money market in equilibrium, so the LM curve **slopes upward**.

explain.alt: A diagram of the IS-LM model. From the initial equilibrium E1 (Y=500, r=4%), when government spending increases and IS1 shifts right to IS2, the equilibrium would be E' (Y=600) if the interest rate stayed at 4%, but in fact the interest rate rises to 6% and equilibrium is reached at E2 (Y=560), producing a crowding-out effect of 40.
explain.caption: Expansionary fiscal policy raises the interest rate and thereby partly crowds out private investment, producing the crowding-out effect.

explain: When the government increases spending and the IS curve shifts to the right, income rises, money demand increases, and the **interest rate rises**. The higher interest rate depresses private investment spending, so the final increase in national income is smaller than the simple multiplier effect. This is called the **crowding-out effect**.

As an extreme exception, in a **liquidity trap** (where the LM curve is horizontal), in which the interest rate is already close to zero and people want to hold only cash instead of bonds, the interest rate does not rise even when income increases. Here monetary policy becomes powerless, while fiscal policy exerts its full multiplier effect without crowding out.

examples.title: Comparing the simple spending multiplier and tax multiplier
body: In an economy with a marginal propensity to consume of $c = 0.75$, we compare raising government spending by 20 with cutting taxes by 20.
Step 1: The government spending multiplier is $\frac{1}{1 - 0.75} = 4$, so $\Delta Y = 80$. Step 2: The tax multiplier is $\frac{-0.75}{1 - 0.75} = -3$, so the tax cut gives $\Delta Y = 60$.
Interpretation: Part of the tax cut (25%) leaks out into saving, so even for the same amount, expanding government spending raises income more.

examples.title: Solving IS-LM equilibrium and calculating crowding out
body: The IS equation is $Y = 700 - 50r$ and the LM equation is $Y = 300 + 50r$.

Step 1: Solving them together gives $100r = 400$, so $r^* = 4(\%)$ and $Y^* = 500$. Step 2: When IS shifts to $Y = 800 - 50r$ because of expanded government spending, the new equilibrium is $r^* = 5(\%)$, $Y^* = 550$.
Interpretation: If the interest rate had stayed at 4%, Y would have been 600 (+100), but as the interest rate rose to 5%, a crowding-out effect of 50 arose and actual income increased by only +50.

eco-11.title: Short-Run and Long-Run Macro Model II: AD-AS and the Phillips Curve
explain: When the price level ($P$) is also treated as a variable, we get the **aggregate demand-aggregate supply (AD-AS) model**. The **aggregate demand (AD) curve** **slopes downward** because when prices rise, the real money supply ($M/P$) falls, the interest rate rises, investment decreases, and net exports fall.

The **short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve** **slopes upward** because, owing to nominal wage rigidity or price misperception, firms increase production when prices rise above what was expected. By contrast, the **long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve** is **vertical** at the **potential output** ($Y_n$) determined by capital, labor, and technology, because all prices and nominal wages adjust flexibly.

In the short run, an inverse relationship appears between the inflation rate ($\pi$) and the unemployment rate ($u$), which is called the **Phillips curve**. Friedman and Phelps introduced **expected inflation** ($\pi^e$) into it and proposed the expectations-augmented Phillips curve $\pi = \pi^e - \alpha(u - u_n) + \nu$ ($u_n$ is the natural rate of unemployment and $\nu$ is a supply shock).

If the government repeatedly expands the money supply to push unemployment below the natural rate ($u_n$), economic agents raise their inflation expectations ($\pi^e$) and demand wage increases. As a result the short-run Phillips curve shifts upward, and **in the long run the unemployment rate returns to the natural rate ($u_n$) and only inflation is higher** (the long-run Phillips curve is vertical).

When a negative **supply shock** ($\nu > 0$) such as a surge in oil prices occurs, the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve shifts to the left (up). This produces **stagflation**, in which a recession (falling output) and rising prices occur together, so aggregate demand management policy alone cannot achieve both goals at once.

examples.title: Calculating inflation with the expectations-augmented Phillips curve
body: Expected inflation is $\pi^e = 2\%$, the natural rate of unemployment is $u_n = 5\%$, the response coefficient is $\alpha = 0.5$, and the supply shock is zero. The current unemployment rate is $u = 3\%$.
Step 1: The unemployment gap is $u - u_n = 3 - 5 = -2(\%p)$. Step 2: $\pi = 2 - 0.5(-2) = 3(\%)$.
Interpretation: In exchange for lowering unemployment 2 percentage points below the natural rate, inflation became 3%, 1 percentage point above expectations.

Interpretation: In long-run equilibrium, output returns to $Y_n = 100$ and only the price level rises further to $P_2 = 106$ (the long-run neutrality of money).

eco-12.title: Long-Run Growth Theory: The Solow Model and Endogenous Growth
explain: A country's long-run standard of living depends on the growth of potential output itself. The **Solow growth model** analyzes the process of accumulation of capital per worker ($k = K/L$). The per-worker production function $y = f(k) = A k^\alpha$ ($0 < \alpha < 1$) is concave and gradually flattens because of the **diminishing marginal product of capital**.

Saving (investment) per worker in each period is $s y = s f(k)$, and the investment required to offset the decline of existing capital due to the depreciation rate ($\delta$) and the population growth rate ($n$) is $(\delta + n)k$. Therefore the change in capital per worker is **$\Delta k = s f(k) - (\delta + n)k$**.

If $s f(k) > (\delta + n)k$ capital grows, and if the opposite holds it shrinks, until capital accumulation stops where the two are equal, **$s f(k^*) = (\delta + n)k^*$**. This is called the **steady state**. A higher saving rate $s$ raises the steady-state level of income per worker ($y^*$), but because of diminishing marginal product, **the long-run growth rate of income per worker in the steady state is 0 regardless of the saving rate** (when there is no technological progress).

The level of capital that maximizes consumption per worker in the steady state, $c^* = f(k^*) - (\delta + n)k^*$, is called the **Golden Rule capital stock**, and it is reached at the point where the slope of the production curve (the marginal product of capital $MPK$) equals $(\delta + n)$ ($MPK = \delta + n$).

In the Solow model, the only source of sustained growth in income per worker is the exogenously given **total factor productivity ($A$), that is, technological progress**. Going beyond this limitation, **endogenous growth theory** (Romer, Lucas) showed that, thanks to the positive externalities of human capital accumulation and research and development (R&D) knowledge, the marginal product of capital does not diminish for society as a whole, so policy and investment can raise the long-run growth rate itself.

examples.title: Calculating the steady state of the Solow model
body: The per-worker production function is $y = k^{0.5}$, the saving rate is $s = 0.3$, the depreciation rate is $\delta = 0.08$, and the population growth rate is $n = 0.02$.

Step 1: Substituting into the steady-state condition $s k^{0.5} = (\delta + n)k$ gives $0.3 k^{0.5} = (0.08 + 0.02)k = 0.1 k$. Step 2: Dividing both sides by $0.1 k^{0.5}$ gives $k^{0.5} = 3$, so $k^* = 9$ and $y^* = 3$.
Interpretation: When capital per worker reaches 9, saving (0.9) exactly matches depreciation plus population dilution (0.9), so capital is maintained.

examples.title: Identifying the Golden Rule saving rate
body: In the economy above ($y = k^{0.5}$, $\delta + n = 0.1$), we find the Golden Rule capital stock $k_{gold}$ that maximizes consumption.

Step 1: Set the marginal product $MPK = 0.5 k^{-0.5} = \delta + n = 0.1$. Step 2: $k^{-0.5} = 0.2 \Rightarrow k^{0.5} = 5$, so $k_{gold} = 25$, and the required saving rate is $s_{gold} = 0.1 \times 25 / 5 = 0.5$.
Interpretation: Long-run consumption per worker is maximized when the marginal product of capital equals the depreciation rate plus the population growth rate.

eco-13.title: Econometrics I: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and Omitted Variable Bias
explain: **Econometrics** is the discipline that tests the causal relationships suggested by economic theory against real data. In the most basic linear regression model $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + u_i$, $X_i$ is the explanatory variable and $u_i$ is the unobserved error term. **Ordinary least squares** (OLS) minimizes the sum of squared residuals $\sum (Y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 X_i)^2$ to obtain the slope estimator $\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\text{Var}(X)}$.

The key condition for the OLS estimator to hit the true value $\beta_1$ without bias, that is, to be an **unbiased estimator** ($E[\hat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1$), is the **exogeneity assumption** $E[u_i | X_i] = 0$, that is, the covariance between the explanatory variable $X$ and the error term $u$ must be 0 ($\text{Cov}(X, u) = 0$). If homoskedasticity and no correlation among errors are added, OLS becomes the **best linear unbiased estimator** (BLUE, the Gauss-Markov theorem), the one with the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators.

In real data, however, the explanatory variable $X$ is frequently correlated with the error term $u$, a problem of **endogeneity** ($\text{Cov}(X, u) \neq 0$). A representative cause is **omitted variable bias** (OVB), in which a third variable $Z$ that should have been included is left out of the model.

Suppose the true model is $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 Z + v$ but we leave out $Z$ and regress $Y$ on $X$ only. The expected value of the estimator is then **$E[\hat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Z)}{\text{Var}(X)}$**. That is, if the omitted variable $Z$ affects the outcome $Y$ ($\beta_2 \neq 0$) and is also correlated with the explanatory variable $X$ ($\text{Cov}(X, Z) \neq 0$), the OLS estimator deviates systematically from the true value.

Besides omitted variables, endogeneity also arises from (1) **reverse causality** (simultaneity), in which $X$ and $Y$ affect each other (for example, police numbers and the crime rate), and (2) **measurement error**, in which observation error is mixed into the explanatory variable. With endogeneity, a serious problem arises: no matter how much the sample size is increased, the estimator does not converge to the true value (inconsistency).

examples.title: Calculating the sign and size of omitted variable bias (OVB)
body: In estimating the effect on wages ($Y$) of years of education ($X$), innate ability ($Z$) was omitted. In the true model $\beta_1 = 5$, the effect of ability is $\beta_2 = 2$, and $\text{Cov}(X, Z) = 6$, $\text{Var}(X) = 4$.
Step 1: Using the bias formula, $\beta_2 \times \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Z)}{\text{Var}(X)} = 2 \times \frac{6}{4} = +3$. Step 2: The expected value of the OLS estimator is $5 + 3 = 8$.
Interpretation: The higher one's ability, the more education one gets and the higher the wage, so if ability is not controlled for, the pure effect of education (5) is overestimated as 8.

examples.title: Finding the OLS slope from the sample covariance and variance
body: In data on advertising spending ($X$) and sales ($Y$), $\text{Cov}(X, Y) = 30$, $\text{Var}(X) = 10$, and the sample means are $\bar{X} = 4, \bar{Y} = 20$.
Step 1: The slope is $\hat{\beta}_1 = 30 / 10 = 3$. Step 2: The intercept is $\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{X} = 20 - 3 \times 4 = 8$.
Interpretation: When advertising spending rises by 1 unit, sales are estimated to increase by 3 units on average.

eco-14.title: Econometrics II: Natural Experiments and Difference-in-Differences (DID)
explain: In the social sciences, where randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are hard to run, a representative quasi-experimental technique for overcoming endogeneity and identifying the pure causal effect of a policy is **difference-in-differences** (DID). It uses data from before and after the policy ($t=0, 1$) for both the **treatment group**, in which the policy was implemented, and the **control group**, in which it was not.

If we look only at the before-and-after difference of the treatment group ($\bar{Y}_{T,1} - \bar{Y}_{T,0}$), a **common time trend**, such as a macroeconomic boom during that period, gets mixed in. Conversely, if we look only at the simple difference between the two groups after the policy ($\bar{Y}_{T,1} - \bar{Y}_{C,1}$), the **inherent gap** between the two groups that existed from the start (selection bias) gets mixed in.

explain.alt: A diagram of difference-in-differences (DID). The treatment group rose by 15, from 50 before the policy to 65 after, and the control group rose by 8, from 40 to 48. Under the parallel trends assumption, the dotted counterfactual for the treatment group is 58, so the pure policy effect (DID) is 15 - 8 = +7 (65 - 58 = +7).
explain.caption: Subtracting the control group's before-and-after change (the common trend) from the treatment group's before-and-after change leaves the pure causal effect.

explain: Difference-in-differences removes these two confounding factors at the same time through two differences. That is, **$\hat{\delta}_{DID} = (\bar{Y}_{T,1} - \bar{Y}_{T,0}) - (\bar{Y}_{C,1} - \bar{Y}_{C,0})$**. In regression form, in $Y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 Post_t + \delta (D_i \times Post_t) + u_{it}$, the coefficient on the interaction term ($D_i \times Post_t$), namely $\delta$, is the DID estimator.

The decisive premise for DID to yield valid causal inference is the **parallel trends assumption**. That is, the assumption that 'had the policy not been implemented in the treatment group, the treatment group would have changed with exactly the same slope as the control group.' Since this assumption cannot be observed directly, one usually checks whether the trends of the two groups were in fact parallel over several periods before the policy (a pre-trend test).

examples.title: Comparing the regression interaction term with the DID table
body: The employment index of a region with a minimum wage increase (treatment $D=1$) changed from 50 to 65, and that of an adjacent region without an increase (control $D=0$) changed from 40 to 48.

Step 1: $\beta_0 = 40$ (control, before), $\beta_1 = 50 - 40 = 10$ (initial group gap), and $\beta_2 = 48 - 40 = 8$ (common time trend). Step 2: The interaction coefficient is $\delta = (65 - 50) - (48 - 40) = 15 - 8 = +7$.
Interpretation: The pure effect of the policy, after stripping out the initial gap (10) and the natural increase (8), is +7.

examples.title: Diagnosing bias when the parallel trends assumption is violated
body: The group participating in job training had, from the start, wage growth that was faster by 30,000 won per year than the group not participating, yet the DID estimate before and after training came out as +100,000 won.

Step 1: The change in the control group does not reflect the treatment group's own additional growth trend (+30,000 won). Step 2: The actual effect of the training is 10 - 3 = 7 (in units of 10,000 won), that is, 70,000 won.
Interpretation: If the treatment group has its own upward trend, the parallel trends assumption is broken and DID overestimates the policy effect.

eco-15.title: Econometrics III: Instrumental Variables (IV) and Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
explain: When unobserved confounders also change over time or reverse causality is at work, difference-in-differences alone has difficulty resolving endogeneity. In such cases, the technique that estimates the causal effect by **picking out only the exogenous variation** in the explanatory variable $X$ that is uncorrelated with the error term $u$ is the **instrumental variables** (IV) method.

For an endogenous explanatory variable $X$, a valid instrument $Z$ must satisfy two conditions. The first is the **relevance condition** ($\text{Cov}(Z, X) \neq 0$), under which the instrument $Z$ must actually move the explanatory variable $X$ significantly. The second is the **exclusion restriction** ($\text{Cov}(Z, u) = 0$), under which $Z$ may influence the outcome only through $X$, reaching $Y$ by no other route: it must not affect $Y$ directly nor be correlated with the error term.

Instrumental variable estimation can be understood intuitively as **two-stage least squares** (2SLS). In the **first-stage regression**, the endogenous variable $X$ is regressed on the instrument $Z$ ($X_i = \pi_0 + \pi_1 Z_i + v_i$) to obtain a predicted value unrelated to the error term $u$, namely $\hat{X}_i$. In the **second-stage regression**, the outcome variable $Y$ is regressed on this clean predicted value $\hat{X}_i$ ($Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{X}_i + \text{오차}$) (오차 means error) to obtain the consistent estimator $\hat{\beta}_{1,IV}$.

In simple regression, the instrumental variable estimator equals the covariance ratio **$\hat{\beta}_{1,IV} = \frac{\text{Cov}(Z, Y)}{\text{Cov}(Z, X)}$**. The numerator $\text{Cov}(Z, Y) / \text{Var}(Z)$ is the reduced-form effect of $Z$ on $Y$, and the denominator $\text{Cov}(Z, X) / \text{Var}(Z)$ is the first-stage regression coefficient ($\hat{\pi}_1$), so in the end **$\hat{\beta}_{1,IV} = \frac{\text{축약형 기울기}}{\text{1단계 기울기}}$** (the Wald estimator; 축약형 기울기 is the reduced-form slope and 1단계 기울기 is the first-stage slope).

One point to note is that if the correlation between the instrument $Z$ and the explanatory variable $X$ is too weak (a **weak instrument**, Weak IV; usually a first-stage $F$-statistic below 10), the denominator approaches 0, the standard error explodes, and the estimator is severely biased. Also, the exclusion restriction cannot be tested directly from the data alone and must be justified by institutional and theoretical context.

examples.title: Finding the IV estimate from the first-stage effect and the reduced-form effect
body: Because of compulsory education rules, birth quarter (instrument Z) raises years of education (X) by 0.4 years on average (first-stage coefficient = 0.4) and raises log wages (Y) by 0.032 (reduced-form coefficient = 0.032).
Step 1: By the exclusion restriction, birth quarter is assumed to affect wages only through years of education. Step 2: $\hat{\beta}_{IV} = 0.032 / 0.4 = 0.08$.
Interpretation: The pure wage-raising effect of one year of education, with endogeneity (innate ability) removed, is about 8% (0.08).

examples.title: Calculating the IV estimate with the covariance formula
body: In estimating the slope of a demand curve, the sample covariances of rainfall (the instrument $Z$ for a supply shock) with price ($X$) and quantity traded ($Y$) are $\text{Cov}(Z, Y) = -12$ and $\text{Cov}(Z, X) = 4$.

Step 1: Rainfall shifts only supply and is unrelated to the demand error term (the exclusion restriction is satisfied). Step 2: $\hat{\beta}_{IV} = \text{Cov}(Z, Y) / \text{Cov}(Z, X) = -12 / 4 = -3$.
Interpretation: Using the shift of the supply curve as an instrument, we identified the slope of the demand curve: when the price rises by 1, the quantity demanded falls by 3.

eco-16.title: International Economics: The Comparative Advantage Trade Model and Exchange Rate Theory
explain: Can a country that is less productive in every field still gain from trade? **Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage** proved that if each country specializes in and exchanges **the good with the lower opportunity cost**, rather than the good with higher absolute productivity, the consumption possibilities of both countries expand. If the opportunity cost of one unit of good $X$ (the amount of good $Y$ given up) is lower than in the other country, the country has a comparative advantage in good $X$.

The **Heckscher-Ohlin model** locates the source of comparative advantage in differences in factor endowments between countries. A labor-abundant country exports labor-intensive goods and a capital-abundant country exports capital-intensive goods. With free trade, the **Stolper-Samuelson theorem** holds: the real return to the abundant factor rises and the real return to the scarce factor falls, which explains the cause of conflict over trade.

When a small country imposes a **tariff** ($t$) on an imported good, the domestic price rises from $P_W$ to $P_W + t$, consumer surplus falls greatly, and only part of it is transferred to domestic producer surplus and government tariff revenue, so a **deadweight loss** equal to two triangles, the consumption distortion and the production distortion, arises.

The long-run level of the **exchange rate** ($E$, the price of one unit of foreign currency in domestic currency), which mediates international transactions, is explained by **purchasing power parity** (PPP, $E = P / P^*$), based on the law of one price. If the domestic inflation rate is higher than the foreign rate, the domestic currency loses value (the exchange rate rises) and real purchasing power is equalized.

In the short-run foreign exchange market, capital movements dominate, so **interest rate parity** (IRP) operates. When the domestic interest rate ($i$) is lower than the foreign interest rate ($i^*$), capital flows are in balance when the domestic currency is expected to strengthen in the future (the exchange rate to fall) by that difference ($i - i^* \approx \frac{E^e - E}{E}$).

examples.title: Comparing opportunity costs and determining comparative advantage
body: Country Alpha takes 2 hours to make 1 bottle of wine and 4 hours to make 1 kg of cheese, and Country Beta takes 6 hours for 1 bottle of wine and 6 hours for 1 kg of cheese.

Step 1: The opportunity cost of 1 kg of cheese is 2 bottles of wine (4/2) in Alpha and 1 bottle of wine (6/6) in Beta. Step 2: The opportunity cost of 1 bottle of wine is 0.5 kg of cheese in Alpha and 1 kg of cheese in Beta.

Interpretation: Alpha has an absolute advantage in both goods, but with respect to the lower opportunity costs, Alpha has the comparative advantage in wine (0.5 < 1) and Beta has it in cheese (1 < 2).

examples.title: Calculating the equilibrium rate of exchange rate change using interest rate parity (UIP)
body: The domestic interest rate is $i = 3\%$ per year, the U.S. interest rate is $i^* = 5\%$ per year, and capital moves freely.

Step 1: Substituting into the interest rate parity condition $i - i^* = (E^e - E)/E$ gives $3\% - 5\% = -2\%$. Step 2: The expected rate of change of the exchange rate must be $-2\%$ for the expected returns on the two currency assets to be equal.

Interpretation: Even if the domestic interest rate is currently 2 percentage points lower, if the KRW/USD exchange rate is expected to fall 2% in the future (the won appreciating 2%), investors are indifferent and equilibrium holds.

eco-17.title: Public Economics: Tax Incidence, Externalities, and Public Goods
explain: On whom the government imposes a tax (legal incidence) and who actually bears the burden (**economic incidence**) are entirely separate questions. When a per-unit specific tax $t$ is imposed, a wedge opens up between the price consumers pay ($P_d$) and the price producers receive ($P_s = P_d - t$), the wedge being of size $t$, and the quantity traded falls.

The division of the tax burden is determined by the **relative size of the price elasticities of demand and supply**. Specifically, the ratio of the consumer burden to the producer burden is **$\frac{\Delta P_d}{\Delta P_s} = \frac{\varepsilon_s}{|\varepsilon_d|}$**. That is, **the less elastic (more inelastic) side, with no substitutes, bears the larger share of the tax**. Also, the more elastic demand or supply is, the greater the fall in the quantity traded due to the tax, and the **excess burden** of the tax (deadweight loss, $\frac{1}{2} t \Delta Q$) grows in proportion to the square of the tax rate ($t$).

The phenomenon in which the market price fails to reflect costs or benefits imposed on third parties is called an **externality**. With a **negative externality** such as pollution, the social marginal cost ($SMC = PMC + MD$, private marginal cost + marginal external damage) is higher than the private marginal cost, so leaving the matter to the market leads to **overproduction** relative to the socially optimal level.

There are two ways to correct this. First, as a government intervention solution, a **Pigouvian tax** imposes a tax exactly equal to the marginal external damage ($MD$) at the socially optimal output, internalizing the external cost into the firm's own costs. Second, the **Coase theorem** shows that if property rights are clearly defined, no matter to whom, and **transaction costs are zero**, voluntary bargaining between the parties alone can reach the socially optimal state.

On the other hand, a good that no one can be excluded from (**non-excludability**) and whose consumption by others does not decrease when one person uses it (**non-rivalry**) is called a **pure public good** (national defense, public safety, and so on). Because of the **free-rider problem**, in which people try to enjoy the benefits without paying, public goods are undersupplied by the market, so the public sector must supply them so that the social marginal benefit, the vertical sum of each person's marginal benefit ($\sum MB_i$), equals marginal cost ($MC$) (the **Samuelson condition**).

examples.title: Calculating elasticity and tax incidence
body: For a certain good, the price elasticity of demand is $|\varepsilon_d| = 0.5$ and the price elasticity of supply is $\varepsilon_s = 1.5$, and a tax of 200 won per unit is imposed.

Step 1: The ratio of the consumer burden to the producer burden is $\varepsilon_s / |\varepsilon_d| = 1.5 / 0.5 = 3 : 1$. Step 2: Dividing 200 won in the ratio 3:1 gives a consumer burden of 150 won and a producer burden of 50 won.
Interpretation: Demand is three times more inelastic than supply, so even if the tax is imposed on producers, consumers bear 75% (150 won).

examples.title: Correcting a negative externality with a Pigouvian tax
body: The market marginal benefit is $MB = 100 - Q$, the firm's private marginal cost is $PMC = 20 + Q$, and the marginal external damage per unit is $MD = 20$.
Step 1: Market equilibrium ($MB = PMC$) is $100 - Q = 20 + Q \Rightarrow Q_m = 40$. Step 2: The social optimum ($MB = PMC + MD = 40 + Q$) is $100 - Q = 40 + Q \Rightarrow Q^* = 30$.
Interpretation: If a per-unit Pigouvian tax t = MD = 20 is imposed, the firm's cost rises to 40 + Q and output falls from 40 to the optimal level of 30.

checks.prompt: A specific tax of 120 won per unit is imposed on a good whose absolute price elasticity of demand is 1.0 and whose price elasticity of supply is 3.0. How many won is the price increase borne by consumers?
checks.hint: The ratio of the consumer burden to the producer burden is supply elasticity (3.0) : demand elasticity (1.0) = 3 : 1.
checks.explanation: Consumers bear 120 won × (3 / (3 + 1)) = 90 won.

checks.prompt: What is the most fundamental reason the Coase theorem has difficulty working for real-world problems such as global warming or air pollution?
checks.hint: The Coase theorem presupposes that 'transaction costs are sufficiently low.'
checks.explanation: When the parties number in the millions, negotiation and monitoring costs (transaction costs) are very large, so voluntary bargaining alone cannot solve pollution.
options: Because the stakeholders are a huge number of unspecified people, so the transaction costs of negotiation are enormous and incentives to free ride arise
Because the externality itself turns positive (+)
Because it is completely prohibited by law for the government to define property rights
Because the marginal external damage is always zero

checks.prompt: To minimize the excess burden (deadweight loss) of taxation when imposing the same tax rate, what kind of good should be taxed (the Ramsey rule)?
checks.hint: Deadweight loss is proportional to 'the amount by which the quantity traded falls (ΔQ)' because of the tax.
checks.explanation: The lower the elasticity, the smaller the distortion of the quantity traded caused by taxation, so deadweight loss is minimized (although fairness concerns about taxing necessities remain).
options: A good whose price elasticity of demand or supply is very low (inelastic)
A good whose demand and supply are both perfectly elastic
A good with very many substitutes, for which consumption plunges when the price rises
A luxury good with no marginal external damage at all

eco-18.title: Asymmetric Information (Adverse Selection and Moral Hazard) and Behavioral Economics
explain: The classical market model assumes that all parties to a transaction share perfect information, but in reality **asymmetric information**, in which one side has more information than the other, is common. Information asymmetry divides into **adverse selection**, which arises from hidden characteristics **before** a contract is made, and **moral hazard**, which arises from hidden actions **after** a contract is made.

Akerlof's **market for lemons (the used car market) model** is a representative case of adverse selection. If buyers cannot distinguish good cars (peaches) from bad cars (lemons) and are willing to pay only the average price, owners of good cars leave the market and only bad cars remain, so that eventually the whole market collapses or shrinks. To mitigate this, sellers must engage in costly **signaling** (for example, quality warranties or educational credentials), or buyers must design **screening** devices (for example, offering a menu of premium and deductible combinations).

**Moral hazard** appears as neglecting fire prevention efforts after buying fire insurance, or as the **principal-agent problem**, in which shareholders (the principal) cannot monitor the manager's (the agent's) effort at every step, so the manager pursues private interests. The solution is to impose a deductible of a certain proportion or to design performance-linked pay (such as stock options) to align incentives.

Meanwhile, **behavioral economics** (Kahneman, Tversky, Thaler) relaxes the assumption that humans are perfectly rational and incorporates actual psychological biases into models. According to **prospect theory**, people evaluate value not by absolute wealth but by gains and losses relative to a **reference point**, and they show **loss aversion**, feeling the pain of a loss more than twice as strongly as the pleasure of a gain of the same amount.

Also common are **hyperbolic discounting** (present bias), in which people overly prefer immediate rewards and postpone future plans, and status quo bias, in which they stay with the default setting. Policy tools that exploit these tendencies to guide desirable behavior through choice design alone (such as changing the default option), without coercion or prohibition, are called **nudges**.

examples.title: Calculating adverse selection in a used-car lemons market
body: A used car market has an even mix of good cars (sellers' minimum acceptable price 10 million won, buyers' willingness to pay 12 million won) and bad cars (sellers 4 million won, buyers 6 million won).

Step 1: The expected willingness to pay of a buyer who does not know the quality is 0.5×12 + 0.5×6 = 9 million won. Step 2: 9 million won is lower than the good-car owners' minimum acceptable price (10 million won), so all good cars are driven out of the market.
Interpretation: In the end only bad cars remain in the market and trade only between 4 and 6 million won, and the mutually beneficial trades of good cars fail to happen.

examples.title: Calculating the loss-averse value function of prospect theory
body: The value of a gain relative to the reference point ($x \ge 0$) is $v(x) = x$, and the value of a loss ($x < 0$) is multiplied by the loss aversion coefficient $\lambda = 2.5$, giving $v(x) = 2.5x$. There is a bet in which a coin is flipped: heads wins 100 won and tails loses 80 won.
Step 1: The objective expected value is $0.5 \times 100 + 0.5 \times (-80) = +10$ won. Step 2: The subjective prospect value is $0.5 \times 100 + 0.5 \times (2.5 \times (-80)) = 50 - 100 = -50$.
Interpretation: Even though it is a favorable bet with a positive expected value (+10 won), the pain of the loss (-200) is greater than the pleasure of the gain (+100), so the bet is declined.

eco-19.title: Bachelor's Capstone I: Integrated Micro, Macro, and Econometric Analysis of Economic Policy Shocks
explain: Now we bring together the tools of microeconomics, macroeconomics, econometrics, and public and international economics to comprehensively diagnose a **composite economic policy shock**. Consider a scenario in which the government imposes a **carbon tax** (a specific tax) on energy to reduce carbon emissions and uses the tax revenue to increase fiscal spending.

**Stage 1 (micro and public economics analysis)**: If energy demand is inelastic and supply is elastic, the economic incidence of the carbon tax falls mostly on consumers and the consumer price rises. At the same time, the carbon tax works as a **Pigouvian tax** that internalizes the marginal external damage ($MD$) into the price, reducing socially excessive consumption to the optimal level and eliminating the externality deadweight loss.

**Stage 2 (macro and international spillovers)**: A rise in energy prices acts as a negative supply shock ($\nu > 0$) that shifts the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve to the upper left, causing higher prices and lower output. Meanwhile, if government spending is increased with the carbon tax revenue, the IS curve shifts to the right, but the **crowding-out effect** from higher interest rates and the fall in net exports from currency appreciation (a lower exchange rate), the Mundell-Fleming effect, offset part of the multiplier effect.

**Stage 3 (econometric causal evaluation)**: To evaluate after the fact how much the policy actually reduced firms' employment or carbon emissions, a simple before-and-after comparison cannot separate the effect of the business cycle. Therefore endogeneity must be removed using **difference-in-differences** (DID), which compares regions that adopted the policy early with regions that did not, or **instrumental variables** (IV), which exploit exogenous regulatory thresholds.

In this way, a single policy can reach a three-dimensional and balanced conclusion only if it is analyzed simultaneously at three levels: **changes in micro relative prices and incentives → macro aggregate demand, aggregate supply, and exchange rate spillovers → identification of econometric causal effects**.

examples.title: Simultaneously calculating carbon tax incidence and the appropriate Pigouvian tax rate
body: Energy inverse demand is $P_d = 120 - 2Q$, private marginal cost is $P_s = 20 + 2Q$, and the marginal external carbon damage per unit is $MD = 20$.
Step 1: Market equilibrium is $120 - 2Q = 20 + 2Q \Rightarrow Q_m = 25, P_m = 70$. Imposing the Pigouvian tax $t = MD = 20$ gives $120 - 2Q = 40 + 2Q$, so the social optimum is $Q^* = 20$.

Step 2: The consumer price is then $P_d = 80$ and the producer's received price is $P_s = 60$, so consumers and producers split the tax of 20 won exactly in half, 10 won each (because the absolute values of the slopes are equal at 2).

examples.title: The difference-in-differences (DID) emissions reduction effect in the policy region
body: Emissions per firm in the region that adopted the carbon tax (treatment) fell from 100 tons to 75 tons, and over the same period the region without it (control) fell from 95 tons to 85 tons because of an economic slowdown.
Step 1: The treatment group's change is 75 - 100 = -25 tons and the control group's change is 85 - 95 = -10 tons. Step 2: The DID estimator is (-25) - (-10) = -15 tons.
Interpretation: Of the total reduction of 25 tons, 10 tons is due to the economic slowdown (the common trend), and the pure causal reduction effect of the carbon tax is 15 tons.

checks.explanation: The new consumer price is Pd = 100 - 16 = 84, so it rises by 4 from 80 (the supply slope is three times steeper, so producers bear 12 and consumers bear 4).

As income rises, money demand increases, the interest rate rises, and private investment is partly depressed (crowding out)

checks.explanation: Positive (+) selection bias (omitted variable bias) exists, so a simple comparison overestimates the pure causal effect of the subsidy.

The parallel trends assumption is automatically satisfied, so an unbiased estimator is obtained

eco-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone II: Designing Economic Policy and a Causal Evaluation Report
explain: The final task of the bachelor's course in economics is to choose one real-world economic policy topic and write a **policy report that designs the theoretical transmission channels and proposes an empirical evaluation method**. Candidate topics to choose from are (1) introducing a carbon tax or an emissions trading scheme, (2) raising the minimum wage or expanding the earned income tax credit (EITC), (3) cutting the policy interest rate or expanding fiscal spending, and (4) imposing import tariffs or subsidy policies.

A complete economics report consists of five parts. First, **[Problem definition and market diagnosis]**: identify the market failure (externality, monopoly or oligopoly, asymmetric information) or macroeconomic imbalance (unemployment, inflation) that the policy seeks to address. Second, **[Micro incentives and incidence analysis]**: based on price elasticity, substitution and income effects, and marginal cost and marginal revenue conditions, infer changes in the behavior of households and firms, along with economic incidence and deadweight loss.

Third, **[Macro general-equilibrium spillovers]**: distinguish the short-run and long-run effects of the policy on aggregate output, prices, and interest rates through IS-LM, AD-AS, the Phillips curve, exchange rates, or long-run capital accumulation (the Solow model). In particular, always check for **offsetting mechanisms** such as crowding out and adjustment of expected inflation.

Fourth, **[Econometric causal identification design]**: explain why simple regression (OLS) on post-policy data falls into endogeneity (omitted variable bias, reverse causality, selection bias), and concretely design the **treatment and control groups and parallel-trends tests of difference-in-differences (DID)** or the **relevance and exclusion restriction conditions of instrumental variables (IV)** to resolve it.

Fifth, **[Policy limitations and complements]**: point out the trade-off between efficiency (minimizing deadweight loss) and equity (distributive justice), as well as the side effects of asymmetric information (moral hazard, adverse selection), and propose complementary measures. Complete the six-stage bachelor's course through the questions below and the self-check checklist.

examples.title: Overview of an integrated analysis of an EITC expansion
body: Micro: It raises the incentive to work among low-income households, causing a positive (+) substitution effect on labor supply, but beyond a certain income range a negative (-) income effect may appear.

Macro and econometrics: It raises the disposable income of groups with a high marginal propensity to consume, so the short-run multiplier effect is large. The evaluation controls for endogeneity with difference-in-differences (DID) comparing households just before and after the household-size threshold.

examples.title: Key self-check criteria for the report
body: 1. Did you avoid confusing legal incidence with economic incidence? 2. Did you distinguish short-run effects (price rigidity) from long-run effects (expectations and wage adjustment)? 3. Did you distinguish correlation from causation and state the identifying assumption (parallel trends or the exclusion restriction)?

Econometric evaluation design to overcome endogeneity (DID or IV)], and [5. Limits in efficiency and equity and complementary measures].
